description: The ants.

Odorous House Ant found under potted plants on a inverted railroad tie retaining wall in my backyard in Cookeville, TN.  In the overhead photo, notice that the flattened single node on the petiole is completely hidden by the anterior segment of the gaster.  OHA have been "deemed" the #1 nuisance ant in TN.  They do not build mounds, but will nest in moist shady areas outside, like under logs, bark, stone pavers, siding and patios.  Indoors, nests will usually be near moisture and food sources.  In the winter, these nests may be near warmth, like a water heater.   OHA are opportunistic foragers and nesters and may establish several satelliite nests on properties from one main colony.  They can become very problematic to control, if they reach large numbers in the colony.

description:
Colonies were found under rocks in slightly sandy soil. I was very interested in the behavior of the ants once captured in the Ziplock bag. Two of the ants that I collected came from the same colony. One had a larvae and the other had a little bunch of eggs. The third ant came from a separate colony of the same species and did not have any eggs or larvae. The first two ants came together and sat all of their baggage in a pile. Then they tended to them. I had a Ring-legged Earwig in the same bag and it was near to the pile they had just made. So those two ants both came to the earwig and “attacked” it making it move to the other side of the bag. Then they promptly returned back to the pile. The third ant then came over and also helped tend to the pile even though it was technically an enemy belonging to another competitor colony.

description:
A last-minute trip to the NJ pine barrens from Philadelphia. Cami, Hirdi and Mika wanted to do a few museums in Philly so I ran off to do some iNatting. I checked the internet for good natural areas near Philly and realized the pine barrens were within 30 miles. I went with a trail I found online (Mullica River Trail (yellow blaze), accessible from the parking area next to the Ranger Station at Atsion (marked as Atsion Office on Google Maps). Odorous house ants are a well-known pest ant species in most of the US.  Colonies of these species can be large with many queens and they are very tolerant to heat and cold.  In fact, the colony of ants around this home had also been observed inside the home during the winter when snow was on the ground, thought to be entering through a crack in the foundation or concrete slab below the flooring.  Odorous house ants will readily invade homes for food, especially sweets, but will also eat other insects.  They also will feed on honeydew produced by ornamental pests such as aphids.  Control of these ants is multifaceted using insecticide baits and liquids as well as elimination of food sources which could include eliminating ornamental pests close to the home.​
